rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention pattern will guide a narrower gradient window and targeted slope or temperature adjustments.
Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether full resolution can be maintained with an earlier last peak.
Shorten the gradient another grid step to reduce elution time while testing the resolution margin of the first pair. The 8-minute gradient retained ample resolution and the maximum CRF.
Test the next shorter gradient while keeping solvent endpoints and temperature fixed. The first pair is slope-sensitive but may remain above R = 1.5, preserving the maximum CRF with faster elution.

The 4-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF, but the first pair has little resolution margin for further steepening. Raise temperature to test whether faster elution and favorable selectivity can preserve full resolution.

Higher temperature worsened the critical pair, so test lower temperature to improve selectivity. Narrowing the solvent window moderates the steepness of a 2-minute gradient, targeting faster elution while retaining full resolution.

Raise the final organic fraction one step to accelerate the last peak, which currently elutes during the hold. This tests whether the first pair retains full resolution despite the slightly steeper gradient; injection 6 remains a maximum-CRF fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to restore the shallower slope of injection 6 while retaining the stronger final solvent of injection 7. Test whether this recovers full resolution of the first pair and keeps the last peak below 3 minutes.

Shift both endpoints upward one step, preserving the slope that fully resolved injection 8 while accelerating the last peak. Monitor the first pair for loss of retention or selectivity at the stronger starting solvent.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to shorten late-peak retention and make the gradient shallower. Check whether the first pair remains fully resolved as it approaches the early-elution region.

Raise temperature by one step to accelerate the last peak while testing the first pair's resolution margin. Keep the starting solvent fixed because the earliest peak is already close to the unretained region.

Test one further temperature step to locate the fastest fully resolved condition at these endpoints. The first pair is close to its resolution limit, so injection 11 remains the fallback if this step drops R below 1.5.

Return to the temperature with better first-pair selectivity and test one higher starting-solvent step. This probes whether a narrower gradient can shorten elution while preserving full resolution, or whether early-peak compression sets the limit.

Lower the final organic fraction one step to test whether a shallower gradient restores the critical pair's resolution at 35 C. Keep phi0 at 0.30 because increasing it to 0.35 caused early-peak compression.

Lower both endpoints relative to injection 11 to retain the first pair longer while preserving gradient slope, and return to 30 C where full resolution was achieved. This tests a potentially more robust maximum-CRF alternative with only a small increase in elution time.

Test a shallower gradient at the temperature that best separates the critical first pair. This targets a larger resolution margin while retaining a short run and the maximum CRF; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 16 to move the first pair away from the near-unretained region while retaining favorable low-temperature selectivity. This tests a short, maximum-CRF alternative with better early-peak retention.

Lower the final organic fraction one step to increase the first pair's resolution margin while preserving adequate early retention. Since maximum CRF is already achieved, this tests a more forgiving separation with only a modest expected increase in last-peak time.

Raise temperature one step from injection 16 to shorten late-peak elution while testing whether its shallower gradient preserves more resolution margin than injection 11. This refines the boundary between fully resolved conditions at 30 C and the first-pair failures at 35 C.

Raise temperature one step from injection 18 to shorten the final-solvent hold while using its extra resolution margin to protect the first pair. Injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved method observed, and the maximum CRF is already secured.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a less aggressive gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping all peaks comfortably within 10 minutes. The lower starting organic fraction should also keep the first pair away from the near-unretained region.

Raise temperature one step in the 4-minute method to shorten elution while testing its substantial first-pair resolution margin. This seeks a faster maximum-CRF variant of injection 21 without pushing the early peaks toward unretained elution.

Shift the starting solvent upward one step and use 35 C to balance faster elution against first-pair selectivity. This tests a compact, fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin than the fastest 2-minute method; the maximum CRF is already secured.
Raise temperature by 5 C from injection 23 to shorten elution while testing whether the first pair retains full resolution. Injection 11 remains the fastest observed maximum-CRF method.
